ch03.title: Five Months Between Nets and Roads
ch03.b002: The week after the twelve gathered in Zebedee’s great house was given over entirely to learning. Each day the six newcomers were placed in the hands of the man who had nominated them, and the older apostles went back over everything they had heard and lived through in the past four months. Matthew was paired with Andrew, Thomas with Philip, Simon with Peter, Judas with Nathaniel. And the twin sons of Alpheus were given to the two sons of Zebedee.
ch03.b003: For the twins it was a happy week, and a sweaty one. John Zebedee was two years younger than they were, but his words were far harder. He tried to repeat to them, without a syllable out of place, what the Master had said about the Father, and the twins lost every syllable. At last James Zebedee could stand it no longer and stopped his brother. Then he told them again in his own way: the Father in heaven cared for them the way their own father Alpheus did, only far, far more. At that the twins nodded. They nodded at the same moment.
ch03.b004: James and Judas Alpheus were twenty-six. They lived near Kheresa, fishing and working the land. Both were married; James had three children, Judas two. Of all the twelve, they were the only two who had not gone through the synagogue schools. They did not hide it. They would not have known how to hide it. When their companions argued at length over some verse of Scripture, the two would sit side by side mending the meshes of a net. Even when they did not know what was being said, they liked being there. It simply made them glad that they had a place among such remarkable men.
ch03.b005: The other pairs each took their own shape. Andrew did not say much to Matthew. He would explain one thing and then wait until Matthew could say it back in his own words. Matthew was grateful for that waiting. Peter and Simon Zelotes both talked so much that it was often impossible to tell who was teaching whom. When their two voices rose on the far side of the garden, the others would exchange glances and laugh. Philip tried to show Thomas everything, one item at a time, and Thomas questioned every item Philip showed him. Strangely, the two of them got along well. Judas learned from Nathaniel. Nathaniel knew a great deal, and he handed over what he knew wrapped in jokes. Judas welcomed the knowledge but not the jokes. Should the work of an apostle be handled so lightly? He did not yet say so aloud.
ch03.b006: In the evenings they all gathered in Zebedee’s garden to hear the Master. In those days Jesus was trying to make one thing plain. What they were to proclaim was the kingdom and its gospel, not himself. They were not to wander off into the bypaths of making legends or building a cult out of beliefs about him and his teachings; they were simply to show forth the Father in heaven. The apostles did not understand why he said this. And no one asked. Instead, he always sent them out with the same words: go and seek the sinners, find the downhearted, and comfort the anxious.
ch03.b007: That week Jesus also set aside a day in the middle of each week for rest. From then on, for the rest of his life, that day was kept, and usually it was Wednesday. On that morning Jesus told them to go out and play for a day. They should lay down the hard labor of the kingdom for a while and enjoy the refreshment of going back to their old work or finding some new kind of recreation. When the twins heard that, they looked at each other. Then, at the same moment, they ran for the shore. That day they stayed in the water until the sun went down. The Master had told them to play, so play they must. That was the only kind of obedience they knew.
ch03.b008: A Question on the First Morning of the Week
ch03.b009: Jesus had planned five months of quiet work, meeting people one at a time. But he did not tell them how long it would last. The apostles lived from week to week. And early on the first day of the week, when the week of training was over, just as Jesus was about to tell the twelve of his plan, three of them came to him first: Simon Peter, James Zebedee and Judas Iscariot.
ch03.b010: Andrew saw the three from across the yard. Peter and James he could understand. But Judas was there between them. A man who had been with them less than ten days was already standing in that place. Andrew could not tell whether it was a good thing or not. It might be zeal. It might be something else.
ch03.b011: Peter drew the Master to one side and spoke boldly. He had come, he said, at the request of his companions. Was the time not ripe now to enter the kingdom? Would the kingdom be proclaimed at Capernaum, or were they to go up to Jerusalem? And when would each of them learn what position he was to hold once the kingdom was set up? Peter would have gone on asking, but Jesus raised his hand. Then he beckoned to the other apostles standing nearby.
ch03.b012: All twelve gathered around. Jesus called them his little children. And he asked how long he must bear with them. Had he not told them many times that his kingdom was not of this world? Had he not said again and again that he had not come to sit on David’s throne? How then could they ask what places they would hold in the Father’s kingdom? They had been called as ambassadors of a spiritual kingdom, he said; soon they would represent him in the world, just as he now represented the Father. They must put out of their minds the idea of a kingdom that ruled by power and reigned in glory. All power in heaven and on earth would soon be given into his hands, but it was not the Father’s will that they use it in this age to exalt themselves. In another age they would indeed sit with him in power and glory; but now they must submit to the Father’s will and go out in humble obedience.
ch03.b013: Once again they were stunned. Peter’s face went white, and James set his mouth hard. Judas bowed his head. Andrew tried to read whether that bowed head meant shame or something else, but he could not. Jesus sent them off two by two to pray and told them to come back to him at noon. Through that heavy morning each of them tried to find God, and each tried to hold up and steady the other. Andrew sat with Matthew on a rock by the shore. For a long time neither spoke. Then Matthew spoke first.
ch03.b014: “I never wanted any position. Being taken in at all is more than enough.”
ch03.b015: Andrew did not answer. But those words held him up all morning.
ch03.b016: At noon they came back. Jesus told them about John’s coming, the baptism in the Jordan, the wedding at Cana, the recent choosing of the six, and how his own brothers in the flesh had drawn away from him. And he warned them that the enemy of the kingdom would try to draw them away too. It was a short talk but a weighty one. When it was over, they all rose, with Peter leading, and declared their unswerving devotion to their Master. Thomas put the pledge in his own way: loyalty to this coming kingdom, whatever it might be, even if he did not fully understand it. Andrew thought that was the most honest thing he had heard all day. They all truly believed in the man. They simply did not yet understand all of his teaching.
ch03.b018: Jesus then asked them how much money they had among them, and what provision had been made for the families they would leave at home. The moment the question was put, Philip began counting in his head. It was his habit. He was twenty-seven and not long married. He had grown up in a fishing family at Bethsaida, the second of seven children. He was not a man who saw far ahead. But what was in front of him, he counted more exactly than anyone.
ch03.b019: The count was soon done. There was not enough money to keep thirteen men for two weeks, even with everything each of them had put in. Philip folded and unfolded his fingers and counted again. The answer was the same. An awkward silence settled over the room. The ambassadors of the kingdom did not have the price of two weeks’ bread.
ch03.b020: Jesus said it was not the Father’s will that they begin their work this way. So they would stay by the sea for two weeks and fish, or do whatever their hands found to do. In the meantime, under the guidance of Andrew, the first chosen, they were to organize themselves and provide for everything their future work would need: not only the present personal ministry, but the time when he would later ordain them to preach the gospel and teach believers.
ch03.b021: At that the room grew bright. Later he would ordain them. It was the first clear sign that one day they would work on a larger scale and in the open. Peter’s face showed he had already forgotten the morning’s rebuke. Philip was glad for another reason. Fishing. That was something he knew. So many fish in a net, so many baskets in a boat, so much money when it went to the drying sheds. He might not understand the kingdom, but fish he could count.
ch03.b022: That afternoon, under Andrew’s direction, they organized themselves. Andrew became chairman. Philip became steward, the one who saw to it that the thirteen, and the visitors and crowds who would come later, had something to eat. Nathaniel was given the care of the apostles’ families. Matthew took charge of finances and of keeping the treasury filled, and Thomas of the itinerary and lodgings. The twins were to keep order among the crowds, and Simon Zelotes was put in charge of rest days and recreation. The man who had talked of uprising in the high councils of the Zealots now had to work out where to take his companions every Wednesday to rest. Nathaniel clapped his hands at the news, and Simon glared at him. But Simon did not do the job carelessly. Whatever he was given, he put his whole heart into it. Soon he would be planning the play and rest of the twelve more thoughtfully than anyone. Judas Iscariot was given the bag. He was to pay all the expenses, keep the books, give Matthew a budget each week, and report to Andrew.
ch03.b023: When his name was called, Philip’s ears went red. Steward. He repeated the word to himself again and again. He knew he was not a man to do great things. He knew, too, what his companions called him: a nickname that meant curiosity. He was always asking to be shown. What he had not seen, he found hard to believe. But this was work he could understand without being shown anything. Bread was bread and fish was fish. That night, before he fell asleep, he was already working out the price of barley for the next week. Thomas could not sleep either. Charged with the itinerary, he was mapping in his head which villages had whose houses and which roads washed out in the rain. Knowing in advance what could go wrong was what he had done all his life. For the first time that habit had found a place where it was useful.
ch03.b025: As the organizing was drawing to a close, Jesus called Andrew. He asked him to choose two or three of his companions to stay at his side, to comfort him and see to his daily needs.
ch03.b026: The moment he heard it, Andrew thought of his own name. He had been the very first to follow: by the roadside at Pella, on the road where they had carried the injured boy home. If it was a matter of staying at the Master’s side, he wanted to raise his hand before anyone. But the Master had just put the whole twelve in his charge. The chief had to stay with the group. He had to notice who was tired, who was missing, in whose house there was sickness. The place beside the Master in night-long prayer and the place of looking after the twelve could not be held by the same man.
ch03.b027: He closed his eyes for a moment. Then he followed the order of their calling. He named the three who had been chosen right after him, Peter, James and John. He called the three and told them of their charge. Peter, overjoyed, threw his arms around his brother. John flushed; James bowed his head low. None of them knew how much their elder had wanted that place. Andrew did not let them know. He liked watching his brother shine in it. He truly did. Only, that night he walked alone along the shore for a long time.
ch03.b028: In later years Andrew would think back often on that choice. In the night vigils of prayer, on the mountain, in conversations no one else knew of, those three were there and he was not. Instead he stayed with the other nine. That was the chief’s place. And he never left it, to the very end.
ch03.b029: For the rest of that day they worked on boats and nets. They had all decided to fish. Most of them had been fishermen before, and the Master himself was an experienced boatman. Many of the boats they used over the next few years had been built with his own hands. They were good and trustworthy boats.
ch03.b031: For two weeks they fished every night in three groups, and each night Jesus went out with a different group. He was a good fisherman. More than that, he was a cheerful companion, and a friend whose presence gave them strength. Nights in the boat with him were the happiest the apostles had known. When the two weeks were over, he told them, they would go out to become fishers of men.
ch03.b032: One night he got into the twins’ boat. At first they did not know what to do. The Master was in the same boat with them; what were they supposed to say? They searched for something to say and in the end said nothing. Instead they did what they always did. They cast the net, waited, and hauled it in. Their hands moved together without a word. For them it was like breathing. The Master spent that night with them.
ch03.b033: Toward dawn the net came up heavy. Silver scales spilled across the bottom of the boat. One of the twins, without meaning to, broke into a broad smile and turned to look at the Master. That was all. There was no teaching and no parable. But the twins never forgot that dawn as long as they lived. Of the words they heard each evening in the garden, they understood less than half. But here in the boat they missed nothing. The Master was doing with them the one thing they knew how to do, and he loved doing it. James Alpheus loved the Master for that simplicity. That dawn he knew that this man spoke the same language he did.
ch03.b034: The more they worked with him in those two weeks, the more they loved him. One day, while folding nets, Matthew said suddenly that with some people, the better you knew them, the less you admired them; but with this man, the less you understood him, the more you loved him. No one disputed it. Not even Thomas.
ch03.b035: On another night, in another boat, Thomas talked with the Master for a long time. He did not tell his companions all of what they said. But from then on he came to see that the Master enjoyed long talks with him. That bewildered him. In his own village no one had wanted to talk with him for long. He argued too much and darkened too easily. Yet this man heard his arguments through to the end. Thomas tried to measure why. Once again he could not.
ch03.b037: When the catch of the two weeks had been sold, Judas Iscariot divided the apostles’ funds into six equal portions; the money for the families had already been set aside. Philip watched Judas’s hands as he divided it. They were quick and exact. Not a single coin went astray. Philip was confident of his own arithmetic, but Judas was a step beyond him. Philip found that more reassuring than enviable.
ch03.b038: It was the twins who actually carried the money to the families. Nathaniel would find out which household needed what, Judas would pay it out, and the twins would take it and set off: to Peter’s house in Bethsaida, to their own homes at Kheresa, to Thomas’s house at Tarichea. They did not think the errand the least bit small. On the contrary, they were proud of it. Walking along with the purse at their belts, they would square their shoulders for no reason at all. When an apostle’s wife opened the door to greet them, when the children ran out and hung on their legs, the twins never doubted that what they were doing was the work of the kingdom. They were the errand boys of the twelve. And they knew it, and were glad.
ch03.b039: In the middle of August they went out two by two to the fields Andrew had assigned them. For the first two weeks Jesus went with Andrew and Peter, for the next two with James and John, and after that with each of the other pairs in the order of their choosing. In this way, before he called them to begin their public ministry, he walked the road at least once with every pair.
ch03.b040: Before they set out, he told them there were three things they were not to talk about: the work and imprisonment of John the Baptist; the voice at the baptism; and the turning of water into wine at Cana. About the voice, only those who had heard it should speak; they were to speak only what they had heard from him, and not pass on hearsay. As for the water and the wine, he charged them strictly to tell no one at all. That charge sank deep into Judas Alpheus. Here was a man who had done so great a thing and told them to say nothing of it, a man who hid his own deeds. Judas Alpheus had never seen humility like that. And within that humility there was a strange dignity.
ch03.b041: What they proclaimed was simple: that sins were forgiven through faith in God, without penance or sacrifice, and that the Father in heaven loved all his children with the same eternal love. That was enough. Philip liked it. There was no need for long explanations. He did not go to people and tell them to do this or do that. He said, let us go together. He said, come and see. The words he had first spoken to Nathaniel had become his way.
ch03.b042: But what Philip learned most in those months was not words. It was the way the Master treated people. In the middle of a deep discussion, if he saw a woman by the road bent under a heavy load, he would go out to her and speak a word of cheer. In the middle of an important conference with the apostles, if a child came up, he would stop and turn to play with the child. The one person in front of him was always the most important. And Philip himself was one of those persons. Sometimes, when the Master was speaking of the deepest things, Philip would break in with some odd question. Only after he had asked it did he realize how odd it was. His companions rolled their eyes. But the Master never once rebuked him. He always answered patiently. Philip all but worshiped that generosity. In this man he could find nothing small, nothing stingy, nothing mean.
ch03.b044: The days of going back and forth, two weeks at the nets and two weeks on the road, were monotonous. And that monotony was a hard test for them. They went through Capernaum and Bethsaida-Julias, Chorazin and Gerasa, Hippos and Magdala, Cana and Bethlehem of Galilee, Jotapata and Ramah, Safed and Gischala, Gadara and Abila. Besides these they passed through countless unnamed villages and fields. There were grumblings, there were doubts, and there were days when hearts went cold for a while.
ch03.b045: Andrew saw it all. When melancholy came over Thomas, he would ask Andrew’s leave to go off by himself for a day or two. Andrew always gave it, and always worried. Thomas soon found out for himself that this was not wise, and that the darker he felt, the better it was to stay at work beside his companions. After that, Thomas stayed instead of leaving. Whatever his mood, he did not let go of the work of an apostle. And whenever news came that someone was sick in one of the apostles’ homes, Nathaniel would get up even in the middle of a council and hurry off. Thanks to him, the twelve could put their worries about home aside.
ch03.b046: Philip had his hard days too. Once night fell in a hill village where no house had bread to spare. The barley loaves in the sack fell far short of thirteen men. Philip went round the village again and again, knocking on doors. That night they each ate half a portion and slept. Philip tossed all night. The steward had let everyone go hungry. But the next morning no one blamed him. In four years there were only a handful of such days. From then on Philip always packed one loaf more than he thought he would need.
ch03.b047: Matthew was often away. Even during the most precious hours of teaching, he had to go out and raise money. Andrew took that to be simply Matthew’s job. Yet there was something strange about it. Even in weeks when the offerings fell short, Judas’s purse never showed its bottom. Something always came in from somewhere, money given in the name of this or that believer. Andrew did not know all those names. He was a good judge of men, but this was one thing he never worked out. Matthew said nothing. When a hint of contempt for the publican flickered in his companions’ eyes, he bit his lip. And the following week he went away again.
ch03.b048: The way Simon Zelotes looked at Matthew changed little by little. For the first few weeks Simon would not take anything Matthew offered him. Then one Wednesday, at an outing Simon had arranged, it was Matthew, of all people, who laughed the loudest. Simon was taken aback for a moment. So a tax collector could laugh like that too. That night the two of them ate from the same pot of stew for the first time. They had not become friends. But they were not enemies either. Judas Iscariot found it uncomfortable to sit alongside Matthew for even longer than Simon did. He simply did not let it show.
ch03.b049: Every week Judas brought his books to Andrew. The books were always clean. The sums always came out. Andrew turned the pages and found nothing to fault. Even so, now and then he found himself looking not at the books but at the hands that held them. He did not know himself what he was looking for. Only, at times, he felt that something beneath all that neatness was sliding off to one side. He gave the feeling no name. What he was not sure of, he did not speak.
ch03.b050: Andrew noticed something in John too. The youngest was quick to draw lines: who belonged to them and who did not, who had the right to speak in the Master’s name and who had not. Andrew knew the hidden conceit of the youngest son. One day, in the years ahead, that same pride would lead John to forbid a stranger who was teaching in the Master’s name. Andrew said nothing about it now. For him, pointing out a fault was as hard as giving praise.
ch03.b051: And what bewildered them most at first was the way the Master treated women. He talked with women freely, and taught that in the kingdom women were to have the same rights as men. Simon Zelotes frowned, Judas kept his mouth shut, and the twins took it as it came. But they soon grew used to it.
ch03.b052: During these same months nearly all the Master’s family drew away from him. Only Ruth, the youngest, stayed at her brother’s side to the end. The others came a few times, but each time it was to try to take him home. They had come close to believing he was out of his mind. When John told the others about it, his voice caught. Andrew thought about brothers who turned their backs on a brother, and then he looked at his own. Peter was by the fire, telling some story with great gusto.
ch03.b054: The year A.D. 26 drew to a close. The persecution that had fallen on John’s followers after his imprisonment died down. For more than five months they had lived this way: two weeks at the nets, two weeks on the road. By the end of it the twelve had made fairly satisfactory arrangements for their families. Most of them were married, and some had children. But now, with a little help from the apostolic funds, they could give themselves to the Master’s work without worrying about home.
ch03.b055: Andrew thought about what those months had left them. Through all the grumbling and doubt and the days when hearts went cold, no one had left. When they first made their pledge, they had pledged themselves to the kingdom. But what held them now was not the kingdom. It was the man: the man who had hauled nets with them, walked the roads with them, slept by the same fires. Each of them had come to regard him as his closest friend in all the world. Not because they understood all his teaching, and not because they had seen wonders. Simply because they had lived with him.
ch03.b056: Andrew saw it in his companions’ faces. However busy he was, Philip filled the Master’s bowl first. When they walked, the twins quarreled over who would walk on either side of him; even their quarrels matched. Matthew wrote down somewhere whatever the Master said. Simon Zelotes still hated Rome, but in the Master’s presence he lowered his voice. Thomas, even on his dark days, never went far from the fire where the Master sat. They loved him for different reasons: one for his generosity, one for his calm, one for his simplicity. But the love itself was the same.
ch03.b057: One evening in early January, Andrew sat by the water at Bethsaida mending a net. A cold wind blew across the lake. In the distance he could hear the twins laughing about something. Philip was over by the drying sheds counting sacks of salt. Andrew called up the faces of the other eleven one by one. And suddenly he realized that the same thing had happened to him. He had served the Master as chief of the twelve: out of duty, out of responsibility, out of the habit of the eldest son. Yet somewhere along the way the man had become his friend. For thirty-three years he had always been the one who looked after someone. He had seldom been anyone’s friend. Andrew stopped his needle. The realization had come so quietly that he had almost missed it.
ch03.b058: He did not know what that friendship would have to bear. He did not know that on the dark days, when reason and judgment and logic all gave way, it would be this friendship that held them to the last. Nor that of the twelve, only one would let go of that cord. Andrew picked up his needle again. In the last few days he had noticed that the Master’s eyes had changed a little. Something was coming. He did not ask what it was. Tomorrow or the day after, when the call came, he would go. The sun went down behind the hills of Galilee. Andrew folded the net and hung it over the side of the boat. He meant to finish mending it in the morning.
ch03.b060: The course of events follows Paper 138, sections 6 to 10. The week in which the older apostles trained the newcomers, the evening teaching in the garden, the midweek holiday, and the charge not to preach about Jesus himself (138:6.1–6.5); the five-month plan and the questions of Peter, James and Judas, Jesus’ rebuke, the prayer in pairs and the return at noon, Thomas’s pledge, the questions about money and families, the two weeks of fishing and the organization, the boats Jesus had built, the fishing in three groups and Matthew’s saying (138:7.1–7.7); the division into six shares and the departure in mid-August, the three forbidden topics, the way Jesus treated people along the road, and the teaching about women (138:8.1–8.11); the five months of testing and the friendship-loyalty they produced, the withdrawal of Jesus’ family, and the towns visited (138:9.1–9.3); and the organization of the apostolic corps (138:10.1–10.11) are drawn from the text. Andrew’s appointment of the three personal aides (139:4.3), the twins’ ages, families and character (139:9.1–9.8), Philip’s nickname, his admiration for the Master’s generosity and his “Come and see” (139:5.2–5.8), Thomas’s going off alone (139:8.11), Nathaniel’s care of the families (139:6.7), Matthew’s secret funding (139:7.8–7.9) and John’s intolerance (139:4.8, with the incident itself at 159:2.1) come from Paper 139.
ch03.b061: Added as fiction are the inner thoughts and feelings of the characters; the specific pairing of elders and newcomers (the text says only that each newcomer was placed with his nominator); the twins playing in the water on Wednesday; the words Andrew and Matthew exchanged on the rock; the dawn in the twins’ boat; the scene in which Andrew hides that he himself wanted the place at the Master’s side (the text says only that he would have liked to volunteer); and small scenes such as the evening by the water in early January. The final scene stops just before January 12, A.D. 27, leading into the next chapter, “The Day of Ordination.”
ch03.b062: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
